claims.content: Precipitate distributions strongly govern alloy strength.
claims.evidence_span: The shape, particle size distribution (PSD) and spatial distribution of precipitates critically influence alloy strength.

claims.content: Fine coherent ordered precipitates strengthen Ni superalloys.
claims.evidence_span: The formation of fine, coherent, ordered, intermetallic precipitates in a face-centered cubic matrix strengthens Ni-based superalloys

claims.content: Inverse transforms can infer PSDs without a preset form.
claims.evidence_span: Rather than beginning with a defined functional form for the PSD, inverse transform approaches seek an arbitrary size distribution that explains the observation

claims.content: LSW specifies a parameterized particle-radius distribution.
claims.evidence_span: LSW theory further specifies a functional form for the PSD characterized by a size parameter to yield a distribution of particle radii r

claims.content: Assuming a PSD shape can bias scattering analysis.
claims.evidence_span: Unfortunately, a priori definition of a defined PSD shape for small-angle scattering (SAS) data analysis can give misleading results.

claims.content: A new precipitate population appeared and coarsened during heat treatment.
claims.evidence_span: During heat treatment, a new population of scatterers appears at high q and shifts to lower q with time, as expected from previous studies of precipitation behavior in this alloy system

claims.content: The dilute-system assumption of LSW may fail in real alloys.
claims.evidence_span: However, some assumptions of LSW theory, such as a dilute system of precipitates, may not apply to real systems.

claims.content: Prior microscopy found spherical small precipitates.
claims.evidence_span: Studies of similar alloys using transmission electron microscopy revealed spherical precipitates on the smallest length scales
